text:
What PCL Is Noticeable?

Below 20 ms (combined total latency): Generally unnoticeable in most single-player experiences, including Cyberpunk. The gameplay remains smooth and responsive.
20-40 ms: Some players might begin to perceive slight lag in input responsiveness, but for slower-paced gameplay (like Cyberpunk), it’s unlikely to be disruptive.
40+ ms: Clearly noticeable, especially in fast camera movements or precise actions (e.g., aiming). It may feel like the game is “lagging behind” your input.

text: This is an incomplete review/uneducated rant.  All the complaints don't realize that ray tracing is not yet at a whole scene calculation like in cinebench r23  It only covers things that the game designer designated for ray tracing which are limited.  That alone had made games better looking.  Now Path tracing takes that ray and bounces it multiple times and calculates how the light is affected based on different textures ...etc.. a true to life simulation (indirect lighting).  This is not meant for games but for renders that are not real time.  The fact that it can even do path ray tracing at 20+ fps even with limited objects...is an huge accomplishment.  We will need another 10 to 15 yrs before we see whole scenes path traced at 30fps in a personal computer with under 1200w consumption

text:
@edrisch8008 
Not at all, you’re misinterpreting what I said. My issue with MFG (Multi-Frame Generation) isn’t just about FPS or raw latency numbers—it’s about the overall experience.

MFG relies on artificially generated frames between real ones, which can introduce visual artifacts and disrupt the natural flow of what’s happening on screen. While some might not notice or care, it’s very apparent for those of us who prioritize a smooth and authentic experience.

As for latency, it’s not just about native FPS. Adding a layer like MFG can make latency less predictable. My criticism doesn’t stem from ignorance—it’s because I expect more from high-end hardware. I want native, authentic performance, not the illusion of smoothness created by artificial frames.

It’s a personal preference, but if MFG works for you, great! I’m just not spending $2000 to rely on a tech like that.

In that case, I'd say you're the fool, or you're just a bourgeois prick who doesn't give a damn about purchasing power and unjustified inflation.

text:
When your frame rate lowers, the latency will exponentially go up. 

This tech isn't going to be terrible on the 5090. Where you're going to find the most issues is on a weaker 5070 card.

The reason the latency will exponentially go up as the frame rate drops, is because of the fact that while the graphics card is rendering frames, it needs to know the 5th frame before it can create the 2nd, 3rd, and 4th frame. At 200fps, you have 1/50th of a second in latency (20ms) just from waiting for the 5th frame to start to be generated, then whatever other latency there is in creating the ai frames, and then natural latency from the card. If the card has a natural latency of 10ms, and let's say it's 2ms per ai frame...

at 200fps, you have 36ms of latency.
Drop that frame rate to 60fps, and  you have 72ms of latency (66.6 from waiting for that 5th frame, 10ms from the card, 2ms per ai frame)

You won't notice the 36ms of latency. You will notice 72ms.

This being said, what is the point of this tech? If you are already seeing near the fps that is required to play your game, then you can put your frame rate way above what your monitor will even show you. This tech is only helpful if it can increase your frame rate from unusable state to a usable state (especially in how they are advertising the 5070)

text:
with all the hate, i think people will still buy the 5090...
the tech is definitely interesting and i hope nvidia will push it in 99% of the games, because let's face it, everyone who knows a bit of tech, will understand that you simply cannot push the raster performance that fast these days.
raster performance usually relies on new fabrication nodes and higher transistor density to pack a lot more of them in the next generation, but now since prices of wafers are high and the new tech doesn't bring nearly as high improvements as it did back in the day, even with only raster improvements in the chip and no RT/Tensor stuff, you would still get barely 30-40% max improvements which is fine, but it's not a generational leap.
dlss 4 on the other hand, completely solves this bottleneck and brings an order of magnitude more performance on the same node as the rtx 4000 series and that's just bonkers really...
sure, there are downsides and cons, like with every approach, as i've just demonstrated above about the raster only focus. so i think FG is here to stay and the fact that i can make from a 35FPS game as 144FPS experience with some slight downgrade on the latency - which, let's face it - you won't feel except maybe in super fast paced games, by super experienced gamers, is...amazing.
rtx 5070 to be able to give me rtx 4090 fps with just dlss 4 at probably 4 times less wattage in a laptop chassis is amazing.

text:
Have to keep it real here, that ghosting is every bit as noticeable as when the game runs on my Series X. Now don't get me wrong, I LOVED this game on my Series X, but for a card that will likely cost most people $2,500+ out the door, I'd expect more. I know it's the industry Halo card, but it's not worth that kind of money. RT on vs off in CP2077 doesn't always look better, it just looks different. Running it on my PC which is no slouch (7800X3D, 7900XTX) I can run this game at all high settings at 4K with FSR Frame Gen and get 125 FPS, which looks great. I've switched to RT and again, it doesn't necessarily look better, just different. Almost too shiny in certain areas and too glossy when it shouldn't be. And please don't say that's because I wasn't using an RTX card. AMD can render RT the exact same as NVIDIA when you're standing still and the visual change has NEVER been worth the performance hit.

I considered getting a 5080 if it was a large improvement over the 4090, but it's not. Too little VRAM (I go over 16GB of VRAM on a bunch of games at 4K, not to mention modded games). I'll spend big money on things like my latest monitor purchase (a 240hz 4K OLED, to replace my LG C2 so I could use it elsewhere), or a 7900XTX, 7800X3D, tons of storage, peripherals, etc etc etc. Can't buy either the 5080 or 5090 out of principle. Hoping UDNA surfaces sooner rather than later to give AMD another top dog option for half the price of NVIDIA.

author: @Buddhakingpen

text:
@Buddhakingpen  People are too closed-minded and can't fathom that there are different types of games with different types of needs.

For a competitive game where high FPS and low latency is important, you'll play the game with DLSS upscaling, no frame-gen, and high base frame-rate (150+). You'll turn on Reflex (half latency) or Reflex 2 when it comes out (quarter latency).

For a high-fidelity single-player game, you'll aim for as much visual fidelity as possible while keeping above 60 FPS with acceptable latency. Some people who are very sensitive to latency might opt to aim for 90 FPS, or 120 FPS. Either way, main goal is not to have amazing latency because single player games are easy as fuck anyway and don't require twitch reactions.

With RTX 50xx, someone with a 240hz monitor can also enjoy a single-player game in 200+ FPS using the new MFG, but the latency would still be similar to a 30/60 FPS game. But picture smoothness will likely be amazing at MFG 200+ FPS.

Basically, ignore the crying children, they are pathetic.

text:
Croatia guy will do that for you, right here, right now 😁
50xx gfx series is capable of calculating multi frames compared to older cards.
As a first action, two raw frames are created because you need those to be able to make/calculate additional (multi)frames which are inserted in-between of the 2 raw frames! 
The more AI frames you have between those 2 raw frames, the more FPS you'll have in total! (Depends also on total raw frames!)
Now, those AI frames inserted between the raw frames are modified to match the motion differences (in one or more steps, depending on DSLL level) between 1st and the 2nd raw frame.
If that is done very efficiently, the less artifacts you'll have. 
Basically, it's a copy-modify-paste process! 
Copy raw frame 1 🖼️ do modification, paste as a AI frame 1, copy that, modify and paste as AI frame 2, copy that, modify and paste as AI frame 3 (here it is important that the changes will connect well to the 2 raw frame 🖼️ and it can be said that AI is working well, but not perfect. Meaning, some artifacts are always there, but not really extremely obvious)
Anyway, you'll have 5 FPS instead of 2!
Latency time, picture quality and AI FPS numbers are of course connected and that is why you'll get, as shown in this video up to    500 FPS (without RTX) or below 50 FPS when not using max. DSLL and with RTX on) and different latency times (it all takes time to calculate, even if DSLL is much faster than raw image calculation)
And you'll get even more different (better) numbers when playing on only 2K screens (1920x1080), instead of 4K (3840x2160) as demonstrated in this vid...
In general:
The less complex raw material is, more raw frames can be generated and that is resulting in more 'fake frames'. Naturally, all is depending on the used DSLL level.
...
Guess, this explains those 'fake frames' ...

text: IMO If you already have a 4090, there's no urgent need to upgrade. However, I believe Nvidia is heading in the right direction. The frames might not be perfect, and there’s some artifacting, but once these issues are addressed and latency is reduced, AI could set a new standard in gaming. The issue with hardware upgrades is that, without AI, performance gains are minimal—only about 5-10%, or 20% at most. This isn’t enough to justify constant new releases. GPUs capable of running 4K 240Hz at high frame rates would be extremely expensive. We’ve reached the limits of hardware improvements, and now the focus needs to shift to AI-driven software, which can optimize efficiency without requiring entirely new hardware each year. This would also ensure that Nvidia can keep cost down making it easier and cheaper to upgrade in the future. So should you buy the 50 series? Well i would if you were on lets say a 3080ti or 3070 or even a 20 series card still. But if you have a 4080, or 4090 i would say maybe a skip until they work out the bugs and whatnot. At the end of the day ask yourself this.. How many games do you play without DLSS on? text:
I usually spend most of my time on the competitive titles like Overwatch or Valorant, but Cyberpunk was one release I hopped onto along with Elden Ring, loving them both tremendously. Also went to 1440p instead of 1080p, 1080p feels ancient in 2025 given how long it's been the 'standard' (and imo, still is with how bad games are optimized on average) but I've committed to going full out, wanting to play my Overwatch with 360hz on max settings if I want, while also wanting to see the best of the best for newer games I haven't really spent the time into.
I'd probably use no framegen (assuming 50ms latency is kinda guaranteed, I do like that the latency doesn't really increase when adding extra frames though!) and use DLSS. I can use DLSS on the max or 1 under max usually and not tell too many issues, and most of that was back on 1080p. I hear it gets even better in higher resolutions, so I think I'm fine relying on DLSS until my card is like 2 generations older and that framegen could make sense in some titles. In competitive titles though? Real excited for reflex 2 and being able to max out everything with minimal lag! Yes, its expensive, but I'm happy to be able to ignore that for once in my life, with my own cash. After this, onto investing for me, really this is my reward for getting out of any sort of debt in the past.

author: @PhilosophicalSock

text:
@PhilosophicalSock  To be fair with Starfield, it only took 2 months for DLSS to be added and in that time the entire gaming community at large, even large publications and media such as Digital Foundry cried foul.

To add, with FSR you can use it no matter the hardware. With DLSS it is tied to specific a company and comes with hardware requirements. 

Dying Light 2 still doesn't have FSR, in any form. Control also still doesn't have FSR. Take a guess as to what these two games have in common. That's right, both are Nvidia sponsored.

The only game that has FSR but not DLSS is RE4 (off the top of my head). You can still use it no matter the GPU though, so it's not a complete loss which is the point I'm making.

Flip the situation and now you've alienated a sizable portion of hardware (including consoles and handhelds), that are without a feature can run your game easier.

Okay, now that aside. The downside to FSR 3.1 is ghosting streaks especially from particles but we're now on version 3.1.3 which includes bug fixes and improvements to the upscaler itself.

AMD is set to release FSR 4, an ML based upscaler and any game that has FSR 3.1 gets upgraded to FSR 4. Had CDPR put in the work earlier then it would have supported the next gen image reconstruction technique day one. 

Every Nixxes port (ratchet and clank, ghost of tsushima) includes upscaling from all 3 hardware companies at close to their latest version, which is why we see Ratchet and Clank with an FSR 4 demo. People over at Nixxes are real talented for them to get that working when CDPR couldn't. But I'll drop that topic since we've been over it.

text:
the only question I havent answered for myself, is which 5090 model i will buy to pair with the 9800x3D pc I built in November. I will def buy one of them, to have the best possible gaming setup. At least until the 6090 and 10800x3D get released. I will upgrade to those, if it gives me a good performance increase. I need and absolutely want every bit of performance I can get, since I have a 32" 4k 240hz QD-OLED monitor, which is obviously incredibly hard to drive.

DLSS Upscaling is ridiculously good, especially at 4k output resolution. DLSS Quality is ALWAYS activated bc it basically looks like native 4k, sometimes even better than that! It always looks better than native 1440p. Obviously. Bc DLSS Quality at 4k means the game renders internally at a native 1440p, and then DLSS fills out the missing pixels through its machine learning algorithm, to get a full 2160p ("4k") image. Remember - 1440p/WQHD is around 3,7 million pixels; 2160p/"4k" is freaking 8,3 million pixels. 

People shouldnt confuse the various features under the DLSS umbrella. Upscaling and Frame Gen and Ray Reconstruction and now Multi Frame Gen are different things. Upscaling is literally always an auto turn on, at least DLSS Quality. Depending on how intensive the game is, you can even go to DLSS Performance aka 1080p internal rendering. DLSS upscaling reduces power usage significantly, reduces GPU-wear, increases performance substantially and it does all that with usually no negatives at all. And if there are minuscule artifacts, they are absolutely worth the MASSIVE performance uplift. But as said, I have yet to see a DLSS Upscaling implementation that makes me turn it off!).

text:
The Frame Generation part is a different story, thats heavily game dependent. It should be seen as a motion fluidity increasing feature, to make a good base frame rate of around 40FPS+ into a way better looking experience through way smoother motion on screen. The higher the base frame rate is, the better Frame Gen works and the less negatives it has. In Black Myth Wukong for example, the Frame Gen is amazing, I always had it on during playing. Max settings, full RT, DLSS Performance (50% res scale) and Frame Gen. Amazing experience. The new multi frame gen will get tested by me. If it looks and feels good, I will use it. If not, I wont. Its also not "FaKe FrAmEs" lmao its LITERAL FRAMES. The frames literally exist. The way they get produced is just different. text:
The latency is very easy to explain, with 25 fps you're looking at 40ms delay without the processing (shown as up to 70 in video). The AI frames doesn't delay the next native frames, it just adds extra frames while it waits for the next native frame, so adding AI frames won't increase the latency at all. You're still playing at only 25 fps from an input perspective, but the visuals show 240 of them.
This also explains why the latency was so low while running with only DLSS on, because the native framerate was higher.

text:
The more you add generated frames, the higher the latency is, but at infinite MFG, the additional latency, assuming perfect scaling (as in generating the frame have 0 cost), will be similar to the cost of rendering a frame. So a 60fps game will have a max latency penalty of 16.7ms (1s divided by 60) assuming you're using infinite MFG. The main contributor for the latency is not the processing cost but the fact that it needs to delay showing the real frame because the need for frame pacing and interpolation. If you search the internet about FSR3 GPU Open, you can see why it introduce additional latency. Basically the game engine render a frame but instead of being shown, it is being hold by half the frame time (assuming it is the normal FG) and then when a new frame is ready being displayed, the game doesn't display that new frame but use that frame + previous frame for interpolation and present the generated frame. The actual new frame will be hold for around half the frame time and you repeat this process. Because the game holding the real frame for half the frame time, normal FG will have an additional 8.3ms for a game with 60fps base frame rate. For 4X MFG, instead of half, it hold the real frame for around 3/4 of the actual frame time, meaning 16.7ms * 0.75 = 12.5ms additional latency or around 4ms higher latency vs 2X FG. Again, all this numbers doesn't take into account the time needed for the game to process the generated frame, but as you can see, while yes, more generated frames add latency, but the subsequent latency increase will be smaller vs the initial latency increase from 2X frame gen.
Basically if you're not bothered with the increased latency from 2x frame gen, 4x frame gen shouldn't bother you in terms of added latency unless we are talking about really low base frame rate.

text:
@fjorddenierbear4832  The 2080ti didn't have that big of a jump, it was closer to 22%.  The increase in raster from the Gtx 908 to the 1080 was 30%, and from the GTX 780 to the GTX 980 was 33% which were crazy numbers for their day.

People forget that the GTX series cards was our path to getting 1080p FHD playable, and that took 6 generations to achieve playable 1080p resolutions across the board.  RTX is all about making 4k the new standard and we are only about to hit our 4th generation in this development cycle.  The 5080 will be to RTX as the 680 was to GTX, and back then I had two GTX 680's in SLI getting like 40fps at 1080p highest settings at best in a lot of titles.  I paid something like $750 each for those GTX 680's and I regularly made them crawl in Arma 2 trying to squeeze every last drop of performance out of them.  It took the GTX 1080 to come out so people could finally play Crysis 3 in full 1080p HD at a then buttery smooth 60fps.

I went from the 1080 to a 2070 Super and can honestly say that it was totally worth it.  The gains were relatively marginal, maybe 20%, but DLSS 2.0 has certainly paid for itself over the last year or two as the card has started showing its age.

The 3090 and 4090's were not an "insane jump" so to speak.  The xx90 cards were not a replacement flagships for the xx80 cards nor replacements for the Titans; 90 cards were always a replacement for having x80 cards run in SLI.  The RTX 3090 was the first gen to bring this idea back since the GTX 690, and although the hardware didn't scale 1:1 on the first (3090) or second (4090) iterations the RTX 5090 is quite literally two RTX 5080's on a single die and PCB.  Fun fact, although the GTX 690 had two GTX 680 dies, sets of VRAM, and so forth on a single PCB it still used SLI technology so both dies shared the  2x2GB VRAM the same way as two separate cards in SLI instead of the new implementation.

text:
@dlarkinc  But, what is the point of dlss4? What's the reasoning? 

They advertise it as bringing the 5070 up to the 4090 in performance. That's just a flat out lie. In any game that the 4090 runs 60fps or lower,  you aren't going to see anywhere near the same performance. Games that the 4090 runs well over 60fps, you'll be able to hit near the same frame rate with a minor latency, but that isn't where people are looking for those gains. They are looking to try to get in that 60-120hz area depending on the game.

If Nvidia just offered this as new tech that was in addition to a big bump in raw performance, I would have no issue with it, but to act like it's just as good as a raw performance increase when in reality, it works great in the situations that you don't need it, but doesn't work ideally in the ones that you do, is just sad.

Where will they stop? I don't see where adding 75% fake frames is going to improve the experience for anyone. I could see adding 1 frame making a game look more smooth. Maybe moving from 120hz to 240hz if you wanted to bump it up to a much better monitor. Will the next 1 be DLSS10, where 90% of the frames are ai generated and we are seeing 1200fps rather than 120? If someone is getting 12FPS, they can get 120fps, but it will look like crap and have terrible latency.

Raster performance and rendering is the (more or less) direct output from the engine to your monitor
When you enable DLSS it's using lower quality textures and upscaling them with some guess work with AI, and it is guess work because if it was native then you wouldn't get a performance boost at all
When you turn on frame gen it's adding extra frames that aren't available natively, which is again guesswork, similar to optical flow for slow motion in an editing software

If it isn't native then it's "fake"
While it's not bad and gets better with every generation, it simply is never going to look as good or be as smooth and seamless as native, it just isn't possible

text:
We've been pushing rasterization for decades, the gains are getting smaller with each new generation. We're at a point where to squeeze out even marginal improvements in rasterization performance, you need exponentially more complex hardware or to throw more transistors at it, which isn't sustainable. The physics of silicon and the practical limits of Moore's Law mean we're not seeing the leaps in raster performance we once did. 

It would actually RAISE the cost of GPU's to attempt pure rasterization, which is something we DON'T WANT. AI can enhance image quality, reduce rendering loads, and make games run smoother at higher resolutions without the proportional increase in rasterized geometry or pixels. This isn't about faking it, it's a smarter way to render and process graphics.

text:
@diligencehumility6971 When exactly were games "so optimized" and FPS "so high"? Back when Crysis launched, I had an 8800 GT, and max settings gave me 30-38 FPS. That was considered decent! Fast forward to now: with a 4080, I’m getting 100-200 FPS in modern AAA games, and enabling DLSS/Frame Generation only pushes it higher.

Back then, hitting 60 FPS meant disabling anti-aliasing, anisotropic filtering, shadows, and other effects. These days, people laugh at 60 FPS, yet there are only 3-5 games at 4K with all optimizations turned off that dip to 34 FPS. Games weren’t more "optimized" back then—they were simpler, and we made huge sacrifices for performance. Now we have tools that let us keep visual quality and performance. That’s progress.
